# The Sima de los Huesos Hominins: A Monograph on the Middle Pleistocene Assemblage of the Sierra de Atapuerca
## 1\. Introduction
The Sima de los Huesos (Pit of Bones) stands as a singularity in the paleoanthropological record, a site of such density and completeness that it has fundamentally altered our understanding of human evolution in the Middle Pleistocene. Located within the intricate karst system of the Sierra de Atapuerca in Burgos, northern Spain, this deep subterranean chamber contains the largest accumulation of hominin fossils ever discovered from a single site in the history of the discipline. The assemblage, currently dated to approximately 430,000 years ago, comprises more than 6,900 identified skeletal elements representing at least 29 individuals .

The significance of the Sima de los Huesos (SH) extends far beyond the sheer quantity of bone. It serves as the primary reference point for understanding the biological and behavioral evolution of the European lineage that eventually gave rise to the Neanderthals. For decades, these fossils resided at the center of a taxonomic storm, oscillating between classifications as *Homo heidelbergensis* and early *Homo neanderthalensis*. The morphological evidence—a mosaic of derived facial traits and primitive neurocranial features—provided the foundation for the "accretion model" of Neanderthal evolution, suggesting that the distinctive anatomy of Late Pleistocene Neanderthals did not appear saltationally but rather accumulated in a modular fashion over hundreds of thousands of years .

In recent years, the site has transcended morphological analysis to become a cornerstone of ancient paleogenomics. The preservation conditions within the deep clay sediments of the Sima allowed for the recovery of both mitochondrial and nuclear DNA from remains nearly half a million years old—the oldest human genetic material ever sequenced. These genomic data have resolved long-standing phylogenetic debates, confirming the SH hominins as early members of the Neanderthal clade while simultaneously revealing complex, ancient interbreeding events with the ancestors of the Denisovans .

Beyond biology, the Sima de los Huesos offers a rare and provocative glimpse into the cognitive and social lives of Middle Pleistocene humans. The demographic profile of the assemblage, the presence of lethal interpersonal violence, and the recovery of a single, exquisitely crafted quartzite handaxe ("Excalibur") have sparked intense debate regarding the origins of mortuary practices and symbolic behavior. If the accumulation is indeed anthropic, as the weight of evidence now suggests, the Sima de los Huesos represents the earliest known manifestation of funerary behavior in the human record .

This report provides an exhaustive synthesis of the research conducted at Sima de los Huesos over the last four decades. It integrates geological, paleontological, taphonomic, and genomic data to construct a comprehensive profile of the SH hominins, their environment, and their place in the human evolutionary tree.

## 2\. Geological and Environmental Setting
### 2.1 The Sierra de Atapuerca Karst System
The Sierra de Atapuerca is a modest limestone range located approximately 15 kilometers east of the city of Burgos, rising to a peak altitude of 1,080 meters above sea level . Despite its seemingly unassuming topography, the Sierra is geologically complex, composed of Cretaceous limestones that have undergone extensive karstification. This process has dissolved the bedrock to create a labyrinthine network of caves, galleries, and vertical shafts (simas) that have acted as sediment traps for millions of years .

The strategic positioning of the Sierra is paramount to its archaeological richness. It sits in the Corridor of La Bureba, a natural geographic bottleneck connecting the drainage basin of the Ebro River (leading to the Mediterranean) with the Duero Basin (leading to the Atlantic). This corridor has served as a primary migratory route for fauna and hominins traversing the Iberian Peninsula for over a million years. The intersection of this migratory highway with the shelter provided by the karst system created an ideal locus for human occupation, resulting in a dense concentration of archaeological sites including Gran Dolina, Sima del Elefante, and the Sima de los Huesos .

### 2.2 The Cueva Mayor-Cueva del Silo Complex
Unlike the open-air sites exposed by the construction of a railway trench (Trinchera del Ferrocarril) in the late 19th century, the Sima de los Huesos is a sealed, deep-cave context. It is located well within the Cueva Mayor-Cueva del Silo system, accessible only by traversing roughly 600 meters of difficult subterranean terrain from the modern entrance of Cueva Mayor .

The site itself is a small chamber at the bottom of a vertical shaft. To reach the fossil deposit, one must navigate through the Sala de los Cíclopes (Hall of the Cyclops) and descend a 13-meter vertical chimney. The chamber at the bottom is physically isolated from the surface, a factor that has played a crucial role in the exceptional preservation of the remains. The environment is characterized by constant humidity, stable temperatures, and a lack of significant water transport, which has protected the DNA within the bones from the rapid degradation typical of fluctuating surface environments .

### 2.3 Stratigraphy and Sedimentology
The stratigraphic sequence of the Sima de los Huesos is distinct from the general cave fill found elsewhere in the system. The deposit is not an occupation layer; there are no hearths, no scattering of lithic debitage, and no processed herbivore bones that would indicate a living floor . Instead, the stratigraphy is defined by a specific accumulation of carnivore and hominin remains encased in a clay-rich mud breccia.

Research by Arsuaga and colleagues has delineated the stratigraphy into distinct lithostratigraphic units. The hominin-bearing layer is a discrete unit, often referred to as Level 6 in the broader context of the sequence or simply the "hominin red clay." This unit is overlaid by layers containing speleothems (calcite formations) and bear remains (*Ursus deningeri*), and underlaid by sterile sands and marls. The separation of the hominin accumulation from the majority of the bear remains—although there is some mixing due to bioturbation—suggests that the human deposition event was distinct from the natural trapping of hibernating bears over millennia .

The sedimentological analysis indicates a low-energy depositional environment. The bones show no signs of rolling or abrasion that would be consistent with transport by high-velocity water flows from the surface. This observation is critical for rejecting the hypothesis that the bodies were washed into the cave by a catastrophic flood event. Instead, the sediments are consistent with the slow accumulation of mud and the in-situ decomposition of bodies in a stagnant, subterranean environment .

### 2.4 Paleoecology of the Middle Pleistocene
The paleoenvironmental reconstruction of the Sierra de Atapuerca during the time of the SH hominins (Marine Isotope Stage 11 or late MIS 12\) suggests a rich and diverse ecosystem. The pollen and faunal records indicate a landscape characterized by open woodland and parkland, supporting a high biomass of herbivores.

The faunal guild included:

* **Large Herbivores:** Rhinoceros (*Stephanorhinus hemitoechus*), wild horses (*Equus ferus*), bison (*Bison priscus*), and diverse cervids (deer). 
* **Carnivores:** The primary competitors for the SH hominins were the Deninger's bear (*Ursus deningeri*), the ancestor of the cave bear; the steppe lion (*Panthera leo fossilis*); the leopard (*Panthera pardus*); and the wolf (*Canis mosbachensis*).

The Sima de los Huesos hominins were apex predators within this guild. Isotopic analyses and the robusticity of their skeletal remains suggest a diet rich in animal protein, acquired through hunting and potentially confrontational scavenging. The presence of such dangerous carnivores in the landscape also contextualizes the risks these hominins faced, although, interestingly, there is no evidence that the bodies in the Sima were preyed upon by lions or wolves prior to their deposition .

## 3\. History of Discovery and Research
### 3.1 The Early Years (1976–1983)
While the archaeological richness of Atapuerca was noted in the late 19th century, the specific location of the Sima de los Huesos remained unknown to science until 1976\. The discovery was made by Trinidad de Torres, a doctoral student in paleontology who was searching for bear fossils to build a biostratigraphic sequence for the region. While excavating in the Cueva Mayor system, Torres recovered the first human fossil from the site: a mandible (Mandible 1\) and several teeth .

This discovery was monumental but initially understated. At the time, the sheer scale of the deposit was unknown. The early excavations led by Emiliano Aguirre in the late 1970s and early 1980s were exploratory, hindered by the extreme difficulty of accessing the site. The shaft required vertical climbing gear, and the extraction of fossils from the cemented breccia in the cramped, air-poor environment was logistically punishing. During this period, the focus of the Atapuerca project was largely divided between the Sima and the newly identified sites in the Railway Trench .

### 3.2 The Golden Age of Excavation (1984–Present)
Systematic, large-scale excavation began in 1984 under the direction of the current leadership team: Juan Luis Arsuaga, Eudald Carbonell, and José María Bermúdez de Castro. The methodology shifted to a surgical removal of sediments, washing and sieving tons of clay to recover even the smallest fragments .

The results were spectacular. In 1992, the team discovered "Agamenón" (Cranium 4\) and "Miguelón" (Cranium 5), the latter being one of the most complete fossil skulls ever found in the world. These discoveries catapulted Atapuerca to global fame and cemented the Sima de los Huesos as a site of "Outstanding Universal Value," leading to its UNESCO World Heritage designation in 2000 .

The volume of material recovered is staggering. By the mid-1990s, the MNI (Minimum Number of Individuals) was estimated at 32, later revised to 28, and most recently to 29 . The inventory includes over 500 teeth, complete pelvises, femurs, and vertebrae. This abundance has allowed researchers to move beyond the description of isolated specimens to the analysis of population biology, variation, and sexual dimorphism in a way that is impossible at almost any other Pleistocene site .

### 3.3 Technological Evolution in Research
The history of research at SH mirrors the technological evolution of paleoanthropology itself.

* **1980s-1990s:** Focus on comparative anatomy, biostratigraphy, and traditional U-series dating. 
* **2000s:** Introduction of CT scanning (Computed Tomography) allowed for the reconstruction of internal cranial structures, inner ear morphology, and virtual endocasts of the brain . 
* **2010s-Present:** The site became the proving ground for ancient DNA research. The successful sequencing of the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes from SH specimens in 2013 and 2016 by the Max Planck Institute marked a paradigm shift, integrating the fossil record with the genomic history of the Denisovans and Neanderthals .

## 4\. Chronology and Dating: Solving the Puzzle
The dating of the Sima de los Huesos has been one of the most contentious and complex chapters in the site's history. The age of the fossils is not merely a number; it dictates the taxonomic identity of the hominins and their relationship to the divergence of modern humans.

### 4.1 The Early "Short Chronology"
In the early years of research (1980s-1990s), the site was tentatively dated to approximately **300,000 to 350,000 years ago**. This estimate was based largely on the biostratigraphy of the microfauna and the evolutionary stage of the *Ursus deningeri* remains. This age placed the hominins comfortably within the later Middle Pleistocene, consistent with their classification as "late" *Homo heidelbergensis* or "pre-Neanderthals" .

### 4.2 The "High Chronology" Controversy
A major disruption occurred in the early 2000s when a study by Bischoff et al., using high-resolution Uranium-series dating on the speleothems (calcite crusts) covering the fossils, proposed a much older date of **\>530,000 years** (and potentially up to 600 ka) .

This "high chronology" created a significant conflict in the field.

* **Morphological Conflict:** If the SH hominins were fully on the Neanderthal lineage at 530 ka, it implied that the split between Neanderthals and modern humans must have occurred much earlier than the 300-400 ka suggested by the genetic molecular clocks available at the time. 
* **Taxonomic Conflict:** Chris Stringer and others argued that 530 ka was too old for fossils with such derived Neanderthal traits. It would imply a rate of evolution inconsistent with other European sites like Mauer or Arago .

### 4.3 The Current Consensus: \~430,000 Years Ago
The conflict was largely resolved in 2014 with the publication of a comprehensive dating study by Arsuaga et al. in *Science*. This study employed a multi-method approach, combining:

1. **Uranium-Series (U-Series) Dating:** On speleothems formed within the mixing of the mud. 
2. **Thermology/Luminescence Dating:** On the sediments themselves (Post-Infrared Infrared Stimulated Luminescence, pIR-IRSL). 
3. **Paleomagnetism:** Analyzing the magnetic polarity of the sediments.

The results converged on a definitive age of **430,000 ± 15,000 years**.1

* **Paleomagnetic Confirmation:** The sediments show **normal magnetic polarity**.16 Since the last major geomagnetic reversal (the Brunhes-Matuyama boundary) occurred at 780,000 years ago, the fossils must be younger than 780 ka. This firmly separates them from the older *Homo antecessor* remains at Gran Dolina (\>780 ka, reversed polarity) . 
* **Biostratigraphic Correlation:** The 430 ka date aligns perfectly with the evolutionary stage of the bears and the microfauna, corresponding to Marine Isotope Stage 11 (MIS 11), a long and stable interglacial period, or the transition from the glacial MIS 12 .

This revised date of 430 ka was the "Goldilocks" solution: old enough to be deep in the Middle Pleistocene, but young enough to fit substantially better with the recalibrated molecular clocks for the Neanderthal-Denisovan split .

## 5\. The Hominin Assemblage: Demography and Preservation
### 5.1 The Largest Fossil Accumulation
The Sima de los Huesos assemblage is, without hyperbole, the most complete fossil record of any Middle Pleistocene population. While other sites yield isolated teeth or fragmented jaws, the Sima has yielded every skeletal element in the human body, from the cranium to the distal phalanges of the toes, including the fragile hyoid bones and auditory ossicles .

The current inventory includes:

* **17 Crania:** Ranging from complete skulls to substantial calvariae. 
* **Mandibles:** Over a dozen nearly complete mandibles. 
* **Teeth:** More than 530 isolated and in-situ teeth . 
* **Postcranial:** Hundreds of vertebrae, ribs, and long bones.

### 5.2 Minimum Number of Individuals (MNI)
The rigorous cataloging of the remains has allowed for a precise estimation of the MNI. As of the most recent census (2020), the MNI stands at **29 individuals**.3 This number is derived from the sorting of element duplication (e.g., finding 29 left femurs) and the association of skeletal parts based on size, age, and morphology.

### 5.3 The Catastrophic Demographic Profile
The age and sex distribution of the 29 individuals is highly anomalous and does not represent a natural mortality profile.

* **The "Prime Age" Bias:** The vast majority of the individuals are adolescents and young adults. Specifically, **82.8%** of the identifiable individuals fall into the adolescent or young adult categories . 
* **Missing Infants:** There is only one individual identified as a child (under 10 years old) . In a natural "attritional" profile (deaths occurring over time in a living group), infants and children usually make up a large percentage of the mortality due to childhood diseases. Their absence here is striking. 
* **Missing Elders:** There are very few older adults. Only four individuals are estimated to be over the age of 30-35, with the oldest perhaps reaching 40-45 years . 
* **Sex Ratio:** The assemblage is balanced between males and females (ratio \~1:1). This refutes early hypotheses that it might have been a group of male hunters or a specific task group .

This demographic profile is termed **"catastrophic."** It suggests that the accumulation does not represent the normal deaths of a group over centuries (which would include many babies and old people). Instead, it implies that these individuals died in a discrete window of time, perhaps due to a specific event or a cultural selection of who was deposited in the pit . This anomaly is central to the "anthropic" (funerary) hypothesis discussed in the Taphonomy section.

## 6\. Cranial Morphology: The "Accretion Model"
The 17 skulls from Sima de los Huesos are the Rosetta Stone for understanding the origin of Neanderthals. They exhibit a distinct morphological pattern that led to the formulation of the "Accretion Model" of evolution. This model posits that Neanderthal traits did not appear all at once in a speciation event but evolved piecemeal—mosaic evolution—beginning with the face and teeth .

### 6.1 Facial Anatomy: The Neanderthal Vanguard
The faces of the SH hominins are unequivocally Neanderthal-like. If one were to look only at the face of "Miguelón" (Cranium 5), it would be difficult to distinguish it from a classic Neanderthal of the Late Pleistocene.

* **Midfacial Prognathism:** The entire midface (nose and maxilla) is pulled forward. This results in a "puffy" appearance around the nose and a retreat of the zygomatic arches (cheekbones) . This prognathism is a key derived Neanderthal trait, likely an adaptation to biomechanical stress from anterior tooth use or climatic adaptation. 
* **Supraorbital Torus:** The brow ridges are massive, double-arched, and continuous across the glabella. This differs from the straight, shelf-like brows of *Homo erectus* and the more interrupted brows of modern humans. The SH brows are hollowed internally by large frontal sinuses, another Neanderthal trait . 
* **Nasal Morphology:** The nasal aperture is large and wide. Internal analysis of the nasal floor and cavity suggests they already possessed the internal nasal structures (turbinates) adapted for conditioning cold, dry air, a hallmark of the Neanderthal lineage's adaptation to glacial Europe .

### 6.2 The Neurocranium: Primitive Retentions
While the face was evolving rapidly toward the Neanderthal condition, the braincase (neurocranium) retained more archaic, primitive features.

* **Cranial Shape:** When viewed from behind (posterior view), the SH skulls have a **pentagonal** or "house-like" profile, with the widest point low on the parietal bones. This contrasts with the spherical, "bomb-like" (en bombe) shape of classic Neanderthals, where the widest point is mid-way up the skull . 
* **Occipital Morphology:** They possess a transverse occipital torus, but it is not as developed into the classic "occipital bun" (chignon) seen in later Neanderthals. It represents an incipient form of this trait .

### 6.3 Cranial Capacity and Encephalization
The brain size of the SH hominins is large compared to *Homo erectus* but smaller than classic Neanderthals and modern humans.

* **Mean Capacity:** The average cranial capacity is approximately **1,232 cc** 22 to **1,241 cc**.5 
* **Range:** The values range from **1,057 cc** (Cranium 6\) to **1,436 cc** (Cranium 4) . 
* **Implications:** This mean is significantly lower than the classic Neanderthal mean of \~1,400 cc. Furthermore, because the SH hominins had very large body masses (discussed below), their **encephalization quotient** (EQ)—the ratio of brain size to body size—is lower than that of Neanderthals. This suggests that the expansion of brain size in the Neanderthal lineage occurred *after* the differentiation of their facial features, a classic example of mosaic evolution .

## 7\. Dental Anthropology: The "Neanderthalization" of the Mouth
The Sima de los Huesos has yielded a treasure trove of dental remains: over 530 teeth, including deciduous (baby) and permanent teeth. The dentition is, perhaps, the most derived system in their biology, showing an advanced degree of "Neanderthalization" .

### 7.1 Dental Morphology
* **Taurodontism:** A defining characteristic of the SH molars is **taurodontism**, a condition where the pulp chamber is vertically enlarged and the roots are fused or short. This trait is rare in modern humans but is a diagnostic feature of Neanderthals . 
* **Shovel-Shaped Incisors:** The upper incisors exhibit strong marginal ridges on the lingual surface ("shoveling") and a swelling at the base (tuberculum dentale). This structural reinforcement is linked to the heavy use of the front teeth as tools . 
* **Posterior Reduction:** The premolars and molars are relatively small compared to the massive anterior dentition. This shift—large front teeth, smaller back teeth—is typical of the Neanderthal face, likely related to the forward projection of the maxilla and the use of the anterior dentition for gripping .

### 7.2 Behavioral Inferences from Teeth
The teeth of the SH hominins are not just anatomical specimens; they are archives of behavior.

* **Paramasticatory Use:** Microscopic analysis of the enamel on the incisors reveals a dense pattern of striations (scratches). These scratches are predominantly oriented in a specific diagonal direction. This pattern is consistent with the "stuff and cut" behavior: gripping meat or hide between the front teeth and cutting it close to the lips with a stone tool. Occasional slips of the tool scratched the enamel . 
* **Handedness:** The angle of these cut marks on the teeth (specifically the right-oblique orientation) indicates that the vast majority of the Sima individuals were **right-handed**. Population-level right-handedness is a uniquely human trait, linked to the lateralization of the brain (dominance of the left hemisphere). Since the left hemisphere also houses the language centers (Broca's and Wernicke's areas), this provides indirect but compelling evidence that the SH hominins possessed the neurological substrate for complex language .

## 8\. Postcranial Anatomy: The "Wide" Body Model
For years, paleoanthropologists struggled to reconstruct the body shape of Middle Pleistocene humans due to the fragmentation of the record. The Sima de los Huesos changed that. With complete pelvises, spines, and limb bones, researchers have reconstructed the "Bauplan" (body plan) of these hominins .

### 8.1 Stature and Mass
Contrary to the popular image of "hunched" cavemen, the SH hominins were tall and incredibly robust.

* **Height:** Estimates based on long bone length suggest a mean stature similar to modern Mediterranean populations, around **170 cm (5'7")** for males and slightly less for females . 
* **Weight:** They were significantly heavier than modern humans of the same height. Males are estimated to have weighed around **90 kg (approx. 200 lbs)** of lean muscle mass. This density implies a caloric requirement significantly higher than that of modern humans .

### 8.2 The "Elvis" Pelvis and the Wide Trunk
The most famous postcranial fossil is Pelvis 1, nicknamed "Elvis." It is the most complete male pelvis in the entire fossil record.

* **Breadth:** The pelvis is extremely wide, with flaring iliac blades. This width dictates the shape of the entire trunk. The SH hominins had a wide, barrel-shaped chest and a massive torso. 
* **Evolutionary Context:** This "wide" body model is now considered the primitive condition for *Homo*. The narrow, cylindrical waist of *Homo sapiens* is a recent adaptation (possibly for endurance running or thermoregulation in tropical Africa). The SH hominins retained the ancestral power-build, which was also efficient for retaining body heat in the temperate/glacial cycles of Europe .

### 8.3 Hand and Foot Morphology
The hands of the SH hominins were powerful, with broad fingertips (apical tufts) for gripping. The thumb morphology suggests they were capable of a "precision grip" (pad-to-pad) essential for making the fine Acheulean tools found in the region. However, the muscular attachments indicate a grip strength far exceeding that of modern humans .

## 9\. Paleogenetics: A Genomic Revolution
The Sima de los Huesos has served as the launchpad for the field of Middle Pleistocene paleogenomics. The recovery of DNA from these fossils is a technical triumph, pushing the boundaries of DNA survival by hundreds of thousands of years.

### 9.1 The Mitochondrial Paradox (2013)
In 2013, Matthias Meyer and his team at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology successfully sequenced the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) from a femur found at the site. The results were shocking.

* **The Finding:** The mtDNA of the Sima hominin did **not** cluster with Neanderthals. Instead, it was closely related to the **Denisovans**, a mysterious sister group of Neanderthals known only from a finger bone in Siberia . 
* **The Paradox:** Morphologically, the SH hominins are early Neanderthals. Genetically (on the maternal line), they appeared to be Denisovans. This created a disconnect between phenotype and genotype.

### 9.2 The Nuclear Resolution (2016)
The paradox was resolved in 2016 when Meyer's team achieved the seemingly impossible: sequencing **nuclear DNA** (nDNA) from two SH specimens. Unlike mtDNA (which is inherited only from the mother), nDNA represents the full ancestry of the individual.

* **The Resolution:** The nuclear DNA confirmed that the Sima de los Huesos hominins were, indeed, members of the **Neanderthal clade**. They shared a common ancestor with Late Pleistocene Neanderthals that was distinct from the Denisovan lineage . 
* **Divergence Dates:** This result proved that the population divergence between Neanderthals and Denisovans must have occurred **before 430,000 years ago**. It pushed the divergence of the "Archaic" lineage (Neanderthals \+ Denisovans) from the Modern Human lineage back to between 550,000 and 765,000 years ago .

### 9.3 Explaining the Mitochondrial Discrepancy
Why did early Neanderthals at Sima carry "Denisovan-like" mtDNA? 
The current hypothesis is that the Sima hominins carried an ancestral form of mtDNA common to both early Neanderthals and Denisovans. Later in the Pleistocene, the Neanderthal population in Europe underwent a bottleneck or a replacement event. A new lineage of mtDNA (possibly introduced by gene flow from an African ancestor related to modern humans) swept through the Neanderthal population, replacing the "Denisovan-like" mtDNA. Thus, the classic Neanderthals of 50,000 years ago carried this "new" mtDNA, while their ancestors at Sima carried the "old" type .

## 10\. Taphonomy: The Mystery of the Pit
The formation of the Sima de los Huesos deposit is the subject of one of the longest-running debates in archaeology. How did 29 bodies end up at the bottom of a dark, inaccessible shaft deep inside a mountain?

### 10.1 Rejected Hypotheses
* **Carnivore Den:** While bear and lion bones are present, the profile does not fit a den. Hyenas, the primary bone accumulators, are absent. The bite marks on the human bones are consistent with scavenging *after* the bodies were already in the pit, likely by bears trapped there . 
* **Living Site:** There is zero evidence of habitation. No stone tools (debitage), no charcoal, no food scraps. The cave is deep, dark, and wet—unsuitable for living . 
* **Catastrophic Geological Transport:** Sediment analysis rules out a high-energy flood washing bodies in from the surface. The bones are not rolled or abraded . 
* **Accidental Fall (Trap):** While the bears likely fell in naturally (attritional accumulation over millennia), the human profile does not fit. A natural trap should catch the clumsy (children) and the weak (elderly). The Sima is full of healthy, prime-age adolescents and young adults. It is statistically improbable that 29 prime-age individuals fell down the same hole accidentally .

### 10.2 The Anthropic Accumulation Hypothesis
The most widely accepted theory today is that the accumulation is **anthropic**—the result of intentional human activity. The Sima de los Huesos was a place of disposal for the dead.

* **Mechanism:** Conspecifics (other group members) dropped the bodies of the deceased down the shaft of the Sima. The shaft acted as a natural disposal chute. 
* **Motivation:** This could be hygienic (to keep rotting corpses away from the living area) or symbolic (a funerary ritual).

### 10.3 The "Excalibur" Handaxe
Supporting the symbolic hypothesis is the discovery of a single lithic artifact among the bones: a handaxe carved from reddish-quartzite, nicknamed **"Excalibur."**

* **Uniqueness:** It is the *only* tool found in the deposit. 
* **Material:** The red quartzite is rare in the Sierra, distinct from the limestone and chert usually used. 
* **Condition:** The edges are sharp and unworn, indicating it was not used heavily or rolled by water. 
* **Interpretation:** Its association with the bodies, in the absence of any other refuse, strongly suggests it was a **grave good**—a symbolic offering deposited with the dead. If accepted, this pushes the origin of symbolic mortuary behavior back to 430,000 years ago, challenging the view that such complexity is unique to *Homo sapiens*.5

### 10.4 Lethal Interpersonal Violence: The First Murder?
The analysis of **Cranium 17** provides a darker context to the accumulation. This skull bears two depressed fractures on the frontal bone (forehead).

* **Forensic Analysis:** The fractures are identical in shape, implying distinct blows from the same object. The trajectory indicates a face-to-face confrontation. 
* **Conclusion:** This is a clear case of **lethal interpersonal violence**—murder. The individual was killed and then deposited in the pit. This confirms that the bodies did not just "wander in" and die; at least one was a victim of violence whose body was disposed of by others. This reinforces the anthropic accumulation theory .

## 11\. Paleopathology and Social Care
The preservation of the SH fossils allows for a detailed assessment of the health and social behavior of the group.

### 11.1 Cranium 14: Compassion in the Pleistocene
Cranium 14 belongs to a child of about 10-12 years. This individual suffered from **craniosynostosis** (specifically, the premature fusion of the lambdoid suture).

* **Impact:** This condition caused severe deformation of the skull and would have likely resulted in increased intracranial pressure and cognitive/motor delays. 
* **Survival:** The fact that this child survived for over a decade with a visible and debilitating condition implies that the group provided **care and support**. They were not abandoned, despite their inability to contribute fully to the group's subsistence. This is early evidence of human empathy and social welfare .

### 11.2 Cranium 5 ("Miguelón"): The Face of Pain
Miguelón, the most complete skull, tells a story of suffering. The left maxilla shows massive bone remodeling due to a severe dental infection (alveolar abscess) centered on a broken tooth.

* **Consequence:** The infection was so severe it likely caused septicemia (blood poisoning), leading to death. The pain would have been excruciating for months. The survival of this individual during the acute phase of the infection again points to social support—others likely processed food for him or protected him .

### 11.3 Auditory Exostoses
Several individuals (e.g., Cranium 4\) show auditory exostoses—bony growths in the ear canal. In modern humans, this is often seen in swimmers or divers exposed to cold water ("surfer's ear"). While we cannot confirm they were swimming, it suggests interaction with aquatic environments or a genetic predisposition .

## 12\. Taxonomic Synthesis: The Redefinition of *Homo heidelbergensis*
The Sima de los Huesos has forced a rewriting of the taxonomy of the Middle Pleistocene.

### 12.1 The Decline of *Homo heidelbergensis*
For decades, SH was the anchor for the species *Homo heidelbergensis*. However, the genomic and morphological data now confirm that SH is fully on the Neanderthal lineage. If SH is a Neanderthal (albeit an early one), and SH is 430,000 years old, then the type specimen of *H. heidelbergensis* (the Mauer mandible, \~600 ka) becomes problematic.

* **The Split:** Many researchers, including the Atapuerca team, now argue that *H. heidelbergensis* should be restricted to the earlier fossils (like Mauer) or abandoned as a "wastebasket taxon." 
* **New Classification:** The Sima hominins are best classified as **Early Neanderthals** or *Homo neanderthalensis* (early group). They represent the establishment of the Neanderthal clade in Europe, distinct from the African lineage that would lead to *Homo sapiens*.17

## 13\. Conclusion
The Sima de los Huesos is more than a collection of bones; it is a monument to a lost humanity. Through the painstaking work of excavation and the application of cutting-edge science, these 29 individuals have spoken across 430,000 years.

They tell us that the Neanderthal lineage was well-established in Europe long before the classic "Ice Age" Neanderthals appeared. They reveal a world where early humans were large, powerful, and apex predators. They show us that the complexity of the human experience—the capacity for violence, the tenderness of care for the disabled, and the stirrings of symbolic thought in the face of death—is not the exclusive preserve of our species, but a deep heritage shared with our archaic cousins.

As the excavation continues, with more than half the deposit still untouched, the Pit of Bones undoubtedly holds more secrets, waiting to further illuminate the shadowed corridors of our origins.

statements.fact: The Sima de los Huesos (Pit of Bones) stands as a singularity in the paleoanthropological record, a site of such density and completeness that it has fundamentally altered our understanding of human evolution in the Middle Pleistocene.
The Sima de los Huesos is located within the intricate karst system of the Sierra de Atapuerca in Burgos, northern Spain.
This deep subterranean chamber contains the largest accumulation of hominin fossils ever discovered from a single site in the history of the discipline.
The assemblage from Sima de los Huesos is currently dated to approximately 430,000 years ago.
The assemblage from Sima de los Huesos comprises more than 6,900 identified skeletal elements representing at least 29 individuals.
The significance of the Sima de los Huesos (SH) extends far beyond the sheer quantity of bone.
The Sima de los Huesos serves as the primary reference point for understanding the biological and behavioral evolution of the European lineage that eventually gave rise to the Neanderthals.
For decades, the Sima de los Huesos fossils resided at the center of a taxonomic storm, oscillating between classifications as Homo heidelbergensis and early Homo neanderthalensis.
The morphological evidence from Sima de los Huesos—a mosaic of derived facial traits and primitive neurocranial features—provided the foundation for the "accretion model" of Neanderthal evolution.

The accretion model suggests that the distinctive anatomy of Late Pleistocene Neanderthals did not appear saltationally but rather accumulated in a modular fashion over hundreds of thousands of years.
In recent years, the Sima de los Huesos site has transcended morphological analysis to become a cornerstone of ancient paleogenomics.

The preservation conditions within the deep clay sediments of the Sima allowed for the recovery of both mitochondrial and nuclear DNA from remains nearly half a million years old—the oldest human genetic material ever sequenced.
These genomic data have resolved long-standing phylogenetic debates, confirming the SH hominins as early members of the Neanderthal clade.
The genomic data simultaneously revealed complex, ancient interbreeding events with the ancestors of the Denisovans.
Beyond biology, the Sima de los Huesos offers a rare and provocative glimpse into the cognitive and social lives of Middle Pleistocene humans.

The demographic profile of the assemblage, the presence of lethal interpersonal violence, and the recovery of a single, exquisitely crafted quartzite handaxe ("Excalibur") have sparked intense debate regarding the origins of mortuary practices and symbolic behavior.
If the accumulation is indeed anthropic, as the weight of evidence now suggests, the Sima de los Huesos represents the earliest known manifestation of funerary behavior in the human record.
The Sierra de Atapuerca is a modest limestone range located approximately 15 kilometers east of the city of Burgos, rising to a peak altitude of 1,080 meters above sea level.
Despite its seemingly unassuming topography, the Sierra is geologically complex, composed of Cretaceous limestones that have undergone extensive karstification.
This process has dissolved the bedrock to create a labyrinthine network of caves, galleries, and vertical shafts (simas) that have acted as sediment traps for millions of years.
The strategic positioning of the Sierra is paramount to its archaeological richness.
It sits in the Corridor of La Bureba, a natural geographic bottleneck connecting the drainage basin of the Ebro River (leading to the Mediterranean) with the Duero Basin (leading to the Atlantic).
This corridor has served as a primary migratory route for fauna and hominins traversing the Iberian Peninsula for over a million years.

The intersection of this migratory highway with the shelter provided by the karst system created an ideal locus for human occupation, resulting in a dense concentration of archaeological sites including Gran Dolina, Sima del Elefante, and the Sima de los Huesos.
Unlike the open-air sites exposed by the construction of a railway trench (Trinchera del Ferrocarril) in the late 19th century, the Sima de los Huesos is a sealed, deep-cave context.
It is located well within the Cueva Mayor-Cueva del Silo system, accessible only by traversing roughly 600 meters of difficult subterranean terrain from the modern entrance of Cueva Mayor.
The site itself is a small chamber at the bottom of a vertical shaft.
To reach the fossil deposit, one must navigate through the Sala de los Cíclopes (Hall of the Cyclops) and descend a 13-meter vertical chimney.
The chamber at the bottom is physically isolated from the surface, a factor that has played a crucial role in the exceptional preservation of the remains.

The environment is characterized by constant humidity, stable temperatures, and a lack of significant water transport, which has protected the DNA within the bones from the rapid degradation typical of fluctuating surface environments.
The stratigraphic sequence of the Sima de los Huesos is distinct from the general cave fill found elsewhere in the system.
The deposit is not an occupation layer; there are no hearths, no scattering of lithic debitage, and no processed herbivore bones that would indicate a living floor.
Instead, the stratigraphy is defined by a specific accumulation of carnivore and hominin remains encased in a clay-rich mud breccia.
Research by Arsuaga and colleagues has delineated the stratigraphy into distinct lithostratigraphic units.
The hominin-bearing layer is a discrete unit, often referred to as Level 6 in the broader context of the sequence or simply the "hominin red clay."
This unit is overlaid by layers containing speleothems (calcite formations) and bear remains (Ursus deningeri), and underlaid by sterile sands and marls.

The separation of the hominin accumulation from the majority of the bear remains—although there is some mixing due to bioturbation—suggests that the human deposition event was distinct from the natural trapping of hibernating bears over millennia.
The sedimentological analysis indicates a low-energy depositional environment.
The bones show no signs of rolling or abrasion that would be consistent with transport by high-velocity water flows from the surface.
This observation is critical for rejecting the hypothesis that the bodies were washed into the cave by a catastrophic flood event.
Instead, the sediments are consistent with the slow accumulation of mud and the in-situ decomposition of bodies in a stagnant, subterranean environment.
The paleoenvironmental reconstruction of the Sierra de Atapuerca during the time of the SH hominins (Marine Isotope Stage 11 or late MIS 12) suggests a rich and diverse ecosystem.
The pollen and faunal records indicate a landscape characterized by open woodland and parkland, supporting a high biomass of herbivores.
The faunal guild included Large Herbivores such as Rhinoceros (Stephanorhinus hemitoechus), wild horses (Equus ferus), bison (Bison priscus), and diverse cervids (deer).

The primary competitors for the SH hominins were the Deninger's bear (Ursus deningeri), the ancestor of the cave bear; the steppe lion (Panthera leo fossilis); the leopard (Panthera pardus); and the wolf (Canis mosbachensis).
The Sima de los Huesos hominins were apex predators within this guild.
Isotopic analyses and the robusticity of their skeletal remains suggest a diet rich in animal protein, acquired through hunting and potentially confrontational scavenging.
The presence of such dangerous carnivores in the landscape also contextualizes the risks these hominins faced.
There is no evidence that the bodies in the Sima were preyed upon by lions or wolves prior to their deposition.
While the archaeological richness of Atapuerca was noted in the late 19th century, the specific location of the Sima de los Huesos remained unknown to science until 1976.
The discovery was made by Trinidad de Torres, a doctoral student in paleontology who was searching for bear fossils to build a biostratigraphic sequence for the region.
While excavating in the Cueva Mayor system, Torres recovered the first human fossil from the site: a mandible (Mandible 1) and several teeth.
This discovery was monumental but initially understated.
At the time, the sheer scale of the deposit was unknown.
The early excavations led by Emiliano Aguirre in the late 1970s and early 1980s were exploratory, hindered by the extreme difficulty of accessing the site.
The shaft required vertical climbing gear, and the extraction of fossils from the cemented breccia in the cramped, air-poor environment was logistically punishing.
During this period, the focus of the Atapuerca project was largely divided between the Sima and the newly identified sites in the Railway Trench.
Systematic, large-scale excavation began in 1984 under the direction of the current leadership team: Juan Luis Arsuaga, Eudald Carbonell, and José María Bermúdez de Castro.
The methodology shifted to a surgical removal of sediments, washing and sieving tons of clay to recover even the smallest fragments.
The results were spectacular.
In 1992, the team discovered "Agamenón" (Cranium 4) and "Miguelón" (Cranium 5), the latter being one of the most complete fossil skulls ever found in the world.
These discoveries catapulted Atapuerca to global fame and cemented the Sima de los Huesos as a site of "Outstanding Universal Value," leading to its UNESCO World Heritage designation in 2000.
The volume of material recovered is staggering.
By the mid-1990s, the MNI (Minimum Number of Individuals) was estimated at 32, later revised to 28, and most recently to 29.
The inventory includes over 500 teeth, complete pelvises, femurs, and vertebrae.

This abundance has allowed researchers to move beyond the description of isolated specimens to the analysis of population biology, variation, and sexual dimorphism in a way that is impossible at almost any other Pleistocene site.
The history of research at SH mirrors the technological evolution of paleoanthropology itself.
From the 1980s-1990s, the focus was on comparative anatomy, biostratigraphy, and traditional U-series dating.
In the 2000s, the introduction of CT scanning (Computed Tomography) allowed for the reconstruction of internal cranial structures, inner ear morphology, and virtual endocasts of the brain.
From the 2010s-Present, the site became the proving ground for ancient DNA research.

The successful sequencing of the mitochondrial and nuclear genomes from SH specimens in 2013 and 2016 by the Max Planck Institute marked a paradigm shift, integrating the fossil record with the genomic history of the Denisovans and Neanderthals.
The dating of the Sima de los Huesos has been one of the most contentious and complex chapters in the site's history.
The age of the fossils is not merely a number; it dictates the taxonomic identity of the hominins and their relationship to the divergence of modern humans.
In the early years of research (1980s-1990s), the site was tentatively dated to approximately 300,000 to 350,000 years ago.
This estimate was based largely on the biostratigraphy of the microfauna and the evolutionary stage of the Ursus deningeri remains.
This age placed the hominins comfortably within the later Middle Pleistocene, consistent with their classification as "late" Homo heidelbergensis or "pre-Neanderthals."

A major disruption occurred in the early 2000s when a study by Bischoff et al., using high-resolution Uranium-series dating on the speleothems (calcite crusts) covering the fossils, proposed a much older date of >530,000 years (and potentially up to 600 ka).
This "high chronology" created a significant conflict in the field.

If the SH hominins were fully on the Neanderthal lineage at 530 ka, it implied that the split between Neanderthals and modern humans must have occurred much earlier than the 300-400 ka suggested by the genetic molecular clocks available at the time.
Chris Stringer and others argued that 530 ka was too old for fossils with such derived Neanderthal traits.
It would imply a rate of evolution inconsistent with other European sites like Mauer or Arago.
The conflict was largely resolved in 2014 with the publication of a comprehensive dating study by Arsuaga et al. in Science.
This study employed a multi-method approach, combining Uranium-Series (U-Series) Dating on speleothems formed within the mixing of the mud.
The study also combined Thermology/Luminescence Dating on the sediments themselves (Post-Infrared Infrared Stimulated Luminescence, pIR-IRSL).
The study also combined Paleomagnetism, analyzing the magnetic polarity of the sediments.
The results converged on a definitive age of 430,000 ± 15,000 years.
The sediments show normal magnetic polarity.
Since the last major geomagnetic reversal (the Brunhes-Matuyama boundary) occurred at 780,000 years ago, the fossils must be younger than 780 ka.
This firmly separates them from the older Homo antecessor remains at Gran Dolina (>780 ka, reversed polarity).

The 430 ka date aligns perfectly with the evolutionary stage of the bears and the microfauna, corresponding to Marine Isotope Stage 11 (MIS 11), a long and stable interglacial period, or the transition from the glacial MIS 12.

This revised date of 430 ka was the "Goldilocks" solution: old enough to be deep in the Middle Pleistocene, but young enough to fit substantially better with the recalibrated molecular clocks for the Neanderthal-Denisovan split.
The Sima de los Huesos assemblage is the most complete fossil record of any Middle Pleistocene population.

While other sites yield isolated teeth or fragmented jaws, the Sima has yielded every skeletal element in the human body, from the cranium to the distal phalanges of the toes, including the fragile hyoid bones and auditory ossicles.
The current inventory includes 17 Crania, ranging from complete skulls to substantial calvariae.
The current inventory includes over a dozen nearly complete mandibles.
The current inventory includes more than 530 isolated and in-situ teeth.
The current inventory includes hundreds of vertebrae, ribs, and long bones.
The rigorous cataloging of the remains has allowed for a precise estimation of the MNI.
As of the most recent census (2020), the MNI stands at 29 individuals.
This number is derived from the sorting of element duplication (e.g., finding 29 left femurs) and the association of skeletal parts based on size, age, and morphology.
The age and sex distribution of the 29 individuals is highly anomalous and does not represent a natural mortality profile.
The vast majority of the individuals are adolescents and young adults.
Specifically, 82.8% of the identifiable individuals fall into the adolescent or young adult categories.
There is only one individual identified as a child (under 10 years old).
In a natural "attritional" profile (deaths occurring over time in a living group), infants and children usually make up a large percentage of the mortality due to childhood diseases.
Their absence here is striking.
There are very few older adults.
Only four individuals are estimated to be over the age of 30-35, with the oldest perhaps reaching 40-45 years.
The assemblage is balanced between males and females (ratio ~1:1).
This refutes early hypotheses that it might have been a group of male hunters or a specific task group.
This demographic profile is termed "catastrophic."
It suggests that the accumulation does not represent the normal deaths of a group over centuries (which would include many babies and old people).
Instead, it implies that these individuals died in a discrete window of time, perhaps due to a specific event or a cultural selection of who was deposited in the pit.
This anomaly is central to the "anthropic" (funerary) hypothesis discussed in the Taphonomy section.
The 17 skulls from Sima de los Huesos are the Rosetta Stone for understanding the origin of Neanderthals.
They exhibit a distinct morphological pattern that led to the formulation of the "Accretion Model" of evolution.
This model posits that Neanderthal traits did not appear all at once in a speciation event but evolved piecemeal—mosaic evolution—beginning with the face and teeth.
The faces of the SH hominins are unequivocally Neanderthal-like.
If one were to look only at the face of "Miguelón" (Cranium 5), it would be difficult to distinguish it from a classic Neanderthal of the Late Pleistocene.
The entire midface (nose and maxilla) is pulled forward.
This results in a "puffy" appearance around the nose and a retreat of the zygomatic arches (cheekbones).
This prognathism is a key derived Neanderthal trait, likely an adaptation to biomechanical stress from anterior tooth use or climatic adaptation.
The brow ridges are massive, double-arched, and continuous across the glabella.
This differs from the straight, shelf-like brows of Homo erectus and the more interrupted brows of modern humans.
The SH brows are hollowed internally by large frontal sinuses, another Neanderthal trait.
The nasal aperture is large and wide.

Internal analysis of the nasal floor and cavity suggests they already possessed the internal nasal structures (turbinates) adapted for conditioning cold, dry air, a hallmark of the Neanderthal lineage's adaptation to glacial Europe.
While the face was evolving rapidly toward the Neanderthal condition, the braincase (neurocranium) retained more archaic, primitive features.
When viewed from behind (posterior view), the SH skulls have a pentagonal or "house-like" profile, with the widest point low on the parietal bones.
This contrasts with the spherical, "bomb-like" (en bombe) shape of classic Neanderthals, where the widest point is mid-way up the skull.
They possess a transverse occipital torus, but it is not as developed into the classic "occipital bun" (chignon) seen in later Neanderthals.
It represents an incipient form of this trait.
The brain size of the SH hominins is large compared to Homo erectus but smaller than classic Neanderthals and modern humans.
The average cranial capacity is approximately 1,232 cc.
The average cranial capacity is approximately 1,241 cc.
The values range from 1,057 cc (Cranium 6) to 1,436 cc (Cranium 4).
This mean is significantly lower than the classic Neanderthal mean of ~1,400 cc.
Furthermore, because the SH hominins had very large body masses, their encephalization quotient (EQ)—the ratio of brain size to body size—is lower than that of Neanderthals.
This suggests that the expansion of brain size in the Neanderthal lineage occurred after the differentiation of their facial features, a classic example of mosaic evolution.
The Sima de los Huesos has yielded a treasure trove of dental remains: over 530 teeth, including deciduous (baby) and permanent teeth.
The dentition is, perhaps, the most derived system in their biology, showing an advanced degree of "Neanderthalization."
A defining characteristic of the SH molars is taurodontism, a condition where the pulp chamber is vertically enlarged and the roots are fused or short.
This trait is rare in modern humans but is a diagnostic feature of Neanderthals.
The upper incisors exhibit strong marginal ridges on the lingual surface ("shoveling") and a swelling at the base (tuberculum dentale).
This structural reinforcement is linked to the heavy use of the front teeth as tools.
The premolars and molars are relatively small compared to the massive anterior dentition.
This shift—large front teeth, smaller back teeth—is typical of the Neanderthal face, likely related to the forward projection of the maxilla and the use of the anterior dentition for gripping.
Microscopic analysis of the enamel on the incisors reveals a dense pattern of striations (scratches).
These scratches are predominantly oriented in a specific diagonal direction.
This pattern is consistent with the "stuff and cut" behavior: gripping meat or hide between the front teeth and cutting it close to the lips with a stone tool.
Occasional slips of the tool scratched the enamel.
The angle of these cut marks on the teeth (specifically the right-oblique orientation) indicates that the vast majority of the Sima individuals were right-handed.
Population-level right-handedness is a uniquely human trait, linked to the lateralization of the brain (dominance of the left hemisphere).

Since the left hemisphere also houses the language centers (Broca's and Wernicke's areas), this provides indirect but compelling evidence that the SH hominins possessed the neurological substrate for complex language.
For years, paleoanthropologists struggled to reconstruct the body shape of Middle Pleistocene humans due to the fragmentation of the record.
The Sima de los Huesos changed that.
With complete pelvises, spines, and limb bones, researchers have reconstructed the "Bauplan" (body plan) of these hominins.
Contrary to the popular image of "hunched" cavemen, the SH hominins were tall and incredibly robust.
Estimates based on long bone length suggest a mean stature similar to modern Mediterranean populations, around 170 cm (5'7") for males and slightly less for females.
They were significantly heavier than modern humans of the same height.
Males are estimated to have weighed around 90 kg (approx. 200 lbs) of lean muscle mass.
This density implies a caloric requirement significantly higher than that of modern humans.
The most famous postcranial fossil is Pelvis 1, nicknamed "Elvis."
It is the most complete male pelvis in the entire fossil record.
The pelvis is extremely wide, with flaring iliac blades.
This width dictates the shape of the entire trunk.
The SH hominins had a wide, barrel-shaped chest and a massive torso.
This "wide" body model is now considered the primitive condition for Homo.
The narrow, cylindrical waist of Homo sapiens is a recent adaptation (possibly for endurance running or thermoregulation in tropical Africa).
The SH hominins retained the ancestral power-build, which was also efficient for retaining body heat in the temperate/glacial cycles of Europe.
The hands of the SH hominins were powerful, with broad fingertips (apical tufts) for gripping.
The thumb morphology suggests they were capable of a "precision grip" (pad-to-pad) essential for making the fine Acheulean tools found in the region.
However, the muscular attachments indicate a grip strength far exceeding that of modern humans.
The Sima de los Huesos has served as the launchpad for the field of Middle Pleistocene paleogenomics.
The recovery of DNA from these fossils is a technical triumph, pushing the boundaries of DNA survival by hundreds of thousands of years.
In 2013, Matthias Meyer and his team at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology successfully sequenced the mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) from a femur found at the site.
The results were shocking.
The mtDNA of the Sima hominin did not cluster with Neanderthals.
Instead, it was closely related to the Denisovans, a mysterious sister group of Neanderthals known only from a finger bone in Siberia.
Morphologically, the SH hominins are early Neanderthals.
Genetically (on the maternal line), they appeared to be Denisovans.
This created a disconnect between phenotype and genotype.
The paradox was resolved in 2016 when Meyer's team achieved the seemingly impossible: sequencing nuclear DNA (nDNA) from two SH specimens.
Unlike mtDNA (which is inherited only from the mother), nDNA represents the full ancestry of the individual.
The nuclear DNA confirmed that the Sima de los Huesos hominins were, indeed, members of the Neanderthal clade.
They shared a common ancestor with Late Pleistocene Neanderthals that was distinct from the Denisovan lineage.
This result proved that the population divergence between Neanderthals and Denisovans must have occurred before 430,000 years ago.
It pushed the divergence of the "Archaic" lineage (Neanderthals + Denisovans) from the Modern Human lineage back to between 550,000 and 765,000 years ago.
The current hypothesis is that the Sima hominins carried an ancestral form of mtDNA common to both early Neanderthals and Denisovans.
Later in the Pleistocene, the Neanderthal population in Europe underwent a bottleneck or a replacement event.
A new lineage of mtDNA (possibly introduced by gene flow from an African ancestor related to modern humans) swept through the Neanderthal population, replacing the "Denisovan-like" mtDNA.
Thus, the classic Neanderthals of 50,000 years ago carried this "new" mtDNA, while their ancestors at Sima carried the "old" type.
Mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) shows Denisovan-like affinity, indicating a deep ancestral link or complex gene flow; ancestral mtDNA lineage retained in SH but lost in later Neanderthals.
Nuclear DNA (nDNA) shows Neanderthal-like affinity, confirming taxonomic status as early Neanderthals; establishes Neanderthal-Denisovan split >430 ka.
The formation of the Sima de los Huesos deposit is the subject of one of the longest-running debates in archaeology.
While bear and lion bones are present, the profile does not fit a carnivore den.
Hyenas, the primary bone accumulators, are absent.
The bite marks on the human bones are consistent with scavenging after the bodies were already in the pit, likely by bears trapped there.
There is zero evidence of habitation.
No stone tools (debitage), no charcoal, no food scraps were found, indicating it was not a living site.
The cave is deep, dark, and wet—unsuitable for living.
Sediment analysis rules out a high-energy flood washing bodies in from the surface.
The bones are not rolled or abraded.
While the bears likely fell in naturally (attritional accumulation over millennia), the human profile does not fit the accidental fall (trap) hypothesis.
A natural trap should catch the clumsy (children) and the weak (elderly).
The Sima is full of healthy, prime-age adolescents and young adults.
It is statistically improbable that 29 prime-age individuals fell down the same hole accidentally.
The most widely accepted theory today is that the accumulation is anthropic—the result of intentional human activity.
The Sima de los Huesos was a place of disposal for the dead.
Conspecifics (other group members) dropped the bodies of the deceased down the shaft of the Sima.
The shaft acted as a natural disposal chute.
This could be hygienic (to keep rotting corpses away from the living area) or symbolic (a funerary ritual).
Supporting the symbolic hypothesis is the discovery of a single lithic artifact among the bones: a handaxe carved from reddish-quartzite, nicknamed "Excalibur."
It is the only tool found in the deposit.
The red quartzite is rare in the Sierra, distinct from the limestone and chert usually used.
The edges are sharp and unworn, indicating it was not used heavily or rolled by water.
Its association with the bodies, in the absence of any other refuse, strongly suggests it was a grave good—a symbolic offering deposited with the dead.
If accepted, this pushes the origin of symbolic mortuary behavior back to 430,000 years ago, challenging the view that such complexity is unique to Homo sapiens.
The analysis of Cranium 17 provides a darker context to the accumulation.
This skull bears two depressed fractures on the frontal bone (forehead).
The fractures are identical in shape, implying distinct blows from the same object.
The trajectory indicates a face-to-face confrontation.
This is a clear case of lethal interpersonal violence—murder.
The individual was killed and then deposited in the pit.
This confirms that the bodies did not just "wander in" and die; at least one was a victim of violence whose body was disposed of by others.
This reinforces the anthropic accumulation theory.
The preservation of the SH fossils allows for a detailed assessment of the health and social behavior of the group.
Cranium 14 belongs to a child of about 10-12 years.
This individual suffered from craniosynostosis (specifically, the premature fusion of the lambdoid suture).
This condition caused severe deformation of the skull and would have likely resulted in increased intracranial pressure and cognitive/motor delays.
The fact that this child survived for over a decade with a visible and debilitating condition implies that the group provided care and support.
They were not abandoned, despite their inability to contribute fully to the group's subsistence.
This is early evidence of human empathy and social welfare.
Miguelón, the most complete skull, tells a story of suffering.
The left maxilla shows massive bone remodeling due to a severe dental infection (alveolar abscess) centered on a broken tooth.
The infection was so severe it likely caused septicemia (blood poisoning), leading to death.
The pain would have been excruciating for months.
The survival of this individual during the acute phase of the infection again points to social support—others likely processed food for him or protected him.
Several individuals (e.g., Cranium 4) show auditory exostoses—bony growths in the ear canal.
In modern humans, this is often seen in swimmers or divers exposed to cold water ("surfer's ear").
While we cannot confirm they were swimming, it suggests interaction with aquatic environments or a genetic predisposition.
The Sima de los Huesos has forced a rewriting of the taxonomy of the Middle Pleistocene.
For decades, SH was the anchor for the species Homo heidelbergensis.
However, the genomic and morphological data now confirm that SH is fully on the Neanderthal lineage.
If SH is a Neanderthal (albeit an early one), and SH is 430,000 years old, then the type specimen of H. heidelbergensis (the Mauer mandible, ~600 ka) becomes problematic.
Many researchers, including the Atapuerca team, now argue that H. heidelbergensis should be restricted to the earlier fossils (like Mauer) or abandoned as a "wastebasket taxon."
The Sima hominins are best classified as Early Neanderthals or Homo neanderthalensis (early group).
They represent the establishment of the Neanderthal clade in Europe, distinct from the African lineage that would lead to Homo sapiens.
The Sima de los Huesos is more than a collection of bones; it is a monument to a lost humanity.

They tell us that the Neanderthal lineage was well-established in Europe long before the classic "Ice Age" Neanderthals appeared.
They reveal a world where early humans were large, powerful, and apex predators.

They show us that the complexity of the human experience—the capacity for violence, the tenderness of care for the disabled, and the stirrings of symbolic thought in the face of death—is not the exclusive preserve of our species, but a deep heritage shared with our archaic cousins.

Pelvis 1 ("Elvis") shows Spondylolisthesis (Lumbar), indicating lower back pain and requiring care.

Abstract
--------

After 34 years of research and findings in the Middle Pleistocene site of the Sima de los Huesos (SH) of the Sierra de Atapuerca (Burgos, Spain), we present an update of the estimation of the number of individuals (ENI) identified in the SH hominin assemblage. The last ENI, published in 2004, was 28. Although the number of specimens recovered has almost doubled since then and more complete information is now available, this new analysis suggests that the ENI is 29. Some individuals are still represented by only one or a few teeth and the upper and lower jaws of various individuals have not been completed. We suggest that the amateur cavers, who accessed the SH site for years looking for bear fossils, destroyed a significant number of hominin fossils. Despite this, we have a good picture of the group of hominins represented in the SH assemblage. Because complete corpses were accumulated in SH and it is a closed cavity, it is expected that a significant number of hominin fossils remains to be discovered. According to the previous estimates, the representation of females is greater than that of males. However, the observed sex ratio is not significantly different from the 1:1 ratio. With the exception of the possible presence of a child individual, most of the remaining 28 individuals are teenagers or young adults (24/28 = 0.857). The ages of death of SH hominins appear to conform to a catastrophic profile.

**Keywords:** Sierra de Atapuerca; Sima de los Huesos; age at death; hominins; number of individuals; sex.

4.content:
Significance
------------

The middle Pleistocene Sima de los Huesos (SH) fossil collection provides the rare opportunity to thoroughly characterize the postcranial skeleton in a fossil population, comparable only to that obtained in the study of the Neandertal hypodigm and recent (and fossil) modern humans. The SH paleodeme can be characterized as relatively tall, wide, and muscular individuals, who are less encephalized than both Neandertals and modern humans. Some (but not all) Neandertal derived traits are present, which phylogenetically links this population with Neandertals. Thus, the full suite of Neandertal features did not arise all at once, and the evolution of the postcranial skeleton could be characterized as following a mosaic pattern.

**Keywords:** human evolution, bauplan, postcranial anatomy, Sierra de Atapuerca, phylogeny

Abstract
--------

Current knowledge of the evolution of the postcranial skeleton in the genus _Homo_ is hampered by a geographically and chronologically scattered fossil record. Here we present a complete characterization of the postcranium of the middle Pleistocene paleodeme from the Sima de los Huesos (SH) and its paleobiological implications. The SH hominins show the following: (i) wide bodies, a plesiomorphic character in the genus _Homo_ inherited from their early hominin ancestors; (ii) statures that can be found in modern human middle-latitude populations that first appeared 1.6–1.5 Mya; and (iii) large femoral heads in some individuals, a trait that first appeared during the middle Pleistocene in Africa and Europe. The intrapopulational size variation in SH shows that the level of dimorphism was similar to modern humans (MH), but the SH hominins were less encephalized than Neandertals. SH shares many postcranial anatomical features with Neandertals. Although most of these features appear to be either plesiomorphic retentions or are of uncertain phylogenetic polarity, a few represent Neandertal apomorphies. Nevertheless, the full suite of Neandertal-derived features is not yet present in the SH population. The postcranial evidence is consistent with the hypothesis based on the cranial morphology that the SH hominins are a sister group to the later Neandertals. Comparison of the SH postcranial skeleton to other hominins suggests that the evolution of the postcranium occurred in a mosaic mode, both at a general and at a detailed level.

* * *

Differences in hominin adaptive strategies ([1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r1)) are reflected in the postcranial skeleton, and can be grouped into broad categories of body plan (or bauplans) ([2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r2)), mainly reflecting hominin posture and locomotion. The first of these may represent a partially arboreal, facultative biped, if the genus _Ardipithecus_ (and perhaps _Orrorin_) is included within the hominins. The australopith bauplan (present in both _Australopithecus_ and _Paranthropus_) mainly reflects terrestrial bipedalism, coupled with suspensory and climbing activities ([3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r3)) that could have also been present in _Homo habilis_ ([4](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r4)). In more derived members of the genus _Homo_, the bauplan reflects an obligate terrestrial bipedalism with reduced arboreal capabilities. Within the genus _Homo_ (excluding the enigmatic and insular species _Homo floresiensis_), different bauplans could be present among early representatives, but among the more derived representatives of the genus, two distinct bauplans can be differentiated based upon the body breadth and overall robusticity, with Neandertals showing a “wide” bauplan and modern humans showing a “narrow” bauplan.

Unfortunately, our understanding of the evolution and variation of body size and shape in Pleistocene _Homo_ before the Neandertals is still quite limited due to a fragmentary and geographically and chronologically scattered fossil record. This has resulted in contradictory views for certain specimens (see, for example, ref. [5](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r5) for _H. habilis_). Most interpretations of body size and shape in early Pleistocene _Homo_ have relied on one specific individual: KNM WT-15000 ([6](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r6)), which has heavily influenced the view that the wider, more robust Neandertal bauplan was derived from and likely reflected cold adaptation ([7](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r7)). Further studies ([8](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r8), [9](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r9)) and the discovery of additional fossil evidence ([10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r10), [11](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r11)) support the idea that the original reconstruction of the pelvis of KNM WT-15000, and thus a number of the interpretations based on it, need to be reconsidered.

In the middle Pleistocene, very few individuals preserve partial postcranial skeletons ([12](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r12)), and in most cases only fragmentary remains are found. Although middle Pleistocene populations have been described as exceptionally robust ([13](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r13)), phylogenetic hypotheses are based mainly on the more abundant cranial sample ([14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r14), [15](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r15)). The recent analysis of 17 crania from Sima de los Huesos (SH) points to a mosaic pattern of evolution in the cranium, with facial modification being the first step in the evolution of the Neandertal clade ([16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r16)). The SH postcranial sample offers an unparalleled opportunity to assess both general aspects of body size and shape and the detailed postcranial morphology, avoiding many of the problems associated with grouping geographically dispersed and chronologically disparate samples. The present study aims to clarify the evolution of the body plan in the genus _Homo_ based on the SH postcranial collection, the largest ever found. We will characterize the general body size and shape \[stature, body breadth, body mass, and encephalization quotient (EQ)\] in the SH paleodeme within the context of postcranial evolution in the genus _Homo_. In addition, we focus in particular on whether the detailed morphological traits found throughout the postcranial skeleton follow a mosaic pattern of evolution, as seen in the crania, and whether there have been changes in the _Homo_ bauplan.

The SH Site
-----------

The Sima de los Huesos site is a well-known middle Pleistocene site that has yielded more than 6,700 human fossils dated to _c._ 430 kiloyears (kyr) ([16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r16)). All of the human remains come from the LU-6 lithostratigraphic unit ([17](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r17)). At least 28 individuals of both sexes and diverse ages at death ([18](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r18)) were preserved, fragmented, and mixed with carnivore bones, mainly of _Ursus deningeri_ ([19](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r19)). These fossils have been considered phylogenetically related to the Neandertals based on the skeletal morphology ([14](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r14), [16](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r16), [20](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r20)–[22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r22)). More than half of the sample corresponds to the postcranial skeleton, with all anatomical parts represented, even the tiny distal pedal phalanges.

The current postcranial minimum number of elements (after the 2013 field season) is 1,523, more than double the number published 15 years earlier ([21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r21)) ([_SI Appendix_, Table S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)). Many of these fossils are complete and for most elements at least one complete specimen is preserved ([10](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r10), [22](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r22)–[28](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r28)). A minimum number of 19 individuals based on the femora are represented in the SH postcranial sample, including both immature and adult individuals.

All postcranial bones of the human skeleton are represented, reducing the previous bias against some elements (thorax, hand, and foot bones). This fact strongly suggests that complete human bodies were deposited in SH ([_SI Appendix_, Table S2 and Fig. S1](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)). This is consistent with previous hypotheses of an anthropic origin for this accumulation ([21](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r21)).

General Body Size and Shape, Intrapopulational Variation, and Encephalization
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

### Stature.

The mean stature of the SH hominins has been estimated based on 24 complete long bones from the upper and lower limbs ([26](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r26)). The overall stature \[(male mean + female mean)/2\] of the SH hominins (163.6 cm) is 3.0 cm taller than the mean stature in Neandertals (160.6 cm) ([_SI Appendix_, Table S3](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)).

### Body Mass.

Body mass (BM) can be reconstructed from hominin skeletal remains using both morphometric \[stature and bi-iliac breadth (BIB)\] ([29](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r29)) or mechanical approaches (joint surface size of weight-bearing skeletal elements) ([30](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r30)). The BM of one large male (Pelvis 1 individual) calculated from stature and BIB is between 90.3 and 92.5 kg ([25](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#r25)), and the Pelvis 2 individual seems to be slightly broader ([Fig. 1_A_](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#fig01)). The pooled sex-weighted mean BM estimated from five adult SH femoral heads is 69.1 kg and is 6.3 kg below the Neandertal mean (75.4 kg) ([_SI Appendix_, Table S4 and Fig. S2](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4577189/#d35e691)).
